\title{Which Retraining Policy Wins the Iterated\\Malware-Detection Game?}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Vaishnavi Suryawanshi}
\IEEEauthorblockA{\textit{Department of Computer Science and Engineering}\\
\textit{ME, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning}\\
Email: terabaapbadplayer@gmail.com}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Machine-learning malware detectors are reliably defeated by adaptive evasion,
and a growing body of work responds by casting the interaction as an iterated
game in which the detector is periodically retrained on the adversarial
examples it failed to catch. That framing is now well established; what is not
established is \emph{which retraining policy to adopt}. Existing studies each
propose and evaluate a single defensive mechanism on its own corpus against its
own attacker, so their results are not mutually comparable, and the policy
design space---how often to retrain, on which data, and by what fitting
procedure---has never been varied systematically. We contribute a controlled
factorial study of that space. Using a shared harness in which attacker,
defender, and metrics are held fixed, we cross retraining cadence,
adversarial-data retention, and retraining mode in a balanced $3\times3\times2$
design over five seeds ($90$ runs) on the real EMBER-2018 corpus, against a
frozen-classifier lower bound and a minimax-alternation baseline. Analysis of
variance orders the three factors unambiguously, and counter to common
practice: how the model is refit dominates ($\omega^2=0.566$), what it is refit
on matters far less ($\omega^2=0.076$), and how \emph{often} it is refit is
statistically undetectable ($p=0.65$). Two mechanisms explain the ordering. The
retention effect is a \emph{capacity threshold} rather than a selection
heuristic: raising the replay cap from $200$ to $800$ samples closes the entire
gap to unbounded replay and simultaneously erases any difference between
eviction rules, while below the threshold the intuitive heuristic---mining the
hardest evasions---is the worst available choice. The mode effect is a
progressive collapse: warm-started retraining accumulates contradictory labels
in the benign region until the detector degenerates, in one of three seeds
falling to $0.659$ clean accuracy and misclassifying $87\%$ of unmodified
malware. Its run-to-run variance is $61\times$ that of refitting
($p=3.5\times10^{-5}$). We release the harness, the calibration results that
constrain how such an experiment must be built, and all run artifacts.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
adversarial machine learning, malware detection, adversarial retraining,
co-evolution, reinforcement learning, EMBER, robustness evaluation
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}

Static machine-learning malware classifiers are attractive because they
generalise beyond signatures, and vulnerable for the same reason: the decision
surface that lets them generalise is also searchable. A decade of work has
established that an adversary with query access and a repertoire of
functionality-preserving transformations will eventually find an evasive
variant of a given
binary~\cite{anderson2018rl,quertier2022merlin,song2022mab,demetrio2021exemples}.
Problem-space attacks are practical rather than
hypothetical~\cite{pierazzi2020problemspace}, and the transformations involved
are cheap.

The natural defence is to retrain on what got through. Since 2022 a second wave
of work has formalised this as an \emph{iterated} process in which attacker and
defender alternate, and the question shifts from whether evasion is possible to
whether the defender converges to a robust boundary, oscillates, or remains
permanently
behind~\cite{ebrahimi2022arl,jureckova2026bilevel,tsingenopoulos2024raid}. That
framing is no longer in doubt. What remains open is the engineering question a
vendor actually faces: \emph{given that we will retrain, under what policy?}

The question is unanswered because the existing studies are not comparable to
one another. Each proposes a single defensive mechanism---bilevel
optimisation~\cite{jureckova2026bilevel}, minimax
alternation~\cite{ebrahimi2022arl}, reinforcement-learning-driven problem-space
hardening~\cite{tsingenopoulos2024raid}, or principled adversarial training with
convergence guarantees~\cite{li2024pad}---and evaluates it on its own corpus,
against its own attacker, with its own metrics. A practitioner reading this
literature learns that adversarial retraining helps. They do not learn whether
to retrain nightly or weekly, whether to keep every adversarial sample or only
the most damaging ones, or whether to refit the model or warm-start it. Those
are the decisions that actually get made, and they are precisely the variables
no study varies.

\textbf{Contributions.} This paper is deliberately \emph{not} a new attacker or
a new defence. It is the controlled-comparison layer that the cluster above
lacks.

\begin{itemize}
\item A reusable co-evolution harness with pluggable attacker, defender, and
retraining policy, in which every policy is scored on identical metrics,
including an \emph{oscillation index} separating a defender that has converged
from one still chasing the attacker (Section~\ref{sec:harness}).

\item Four negative calibration results that constrain how such an experiment
must be built at all. Most consequentially, the encoding of \emph{which
features the adversary may modify} silently determines the outcome: under a
common but overly restrictive choice, every retraining policy ties at zero and
the comparison is vacuous (Section~\ref{sec:calibration}).

\item A balanced $3\times3\times2$ factorial study on real EMBER-2018 features
($90$ runs), bounded below by a frozen classifier and compared against a
minimax-alternation baseline, yielding an unambiguous ordering of the three
policy factors (Section~\ref{sec:results}).

\item Mechanistic follow-ups for the two factors that matter: a capacity
threshold for retention, and a detector-collapse mode for warm-started
retraining, the latter established as a variance result rather than an anecdote
(Sections~\ref{sec:capacity} and~\ref{sec:mode}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Single-round evasion.} Anderson \emph{et al.}~\cite{anderson2018rl}
introduced a reinforcement-learning agent over functionality-preserving PE
transformations, evaluated against a frozen classifier.
MERLIN~\cite{quertier2022merlin} extends the algorithm family, and
MAB-Malware~\cite{song2022mab} recasts the search as a multi-armed bandit,
reporting $74$--$97\%$ evasion against static detectors. Demetrio \emph{et
al.}~\cite{demetrio2021exemples} unify these attacks and show many are
query-inefficient, and give a functionality-preserving black-box
optimiser~\cite{demetrio2021tifs}; Pierazzi \emph{et
al.}~\cite{pierazzi2020problemspace} formalise the constraints that make an
attack realisable in the problem space rather than only in feature space. This
line establishes that evasion is achievable, then stops at first success: the
defender never responds.

\textbf{Iterated and game-theoretic formulations.} Ebrahimi \emph{et
al.}~\cite{ebrahimi2022arl} alternate attacker- and detector-strengthening in a
minimax framing. Jure\v{c}kov\'{a} \emph{et al.}~\cite{jureckova2026bilevel}
make the nesting explicit as bilevel optimisation and report near-total
immunity, evasion falling to $0$--$1.89\%$ on three malware families.
Tsingenopoulos \emph{et al.}~\cite{tsingenopoulos2024raid} harden a commercial
antivirus pipeline through the problem space and report a $0\%$ attack success
rate after a few adversarial retraining iterations. Li \emph{et
al.}~\cite{li2024pad} approach the goal from theory, giving adversarial
training convergence guarantees for smooth detectors. Each contributes one
mechanism, evaluated in isolation, and their results cannot be placed on a
common axis: reported evasion rates differ by two orders of magnitude across
papers that all conclude their defence works. That spread is itself the
motivation for a shared harness.

\textbf{Drift-aware retraining.} DRMD~\cite{mcfadden2026drmd} learns when to
classify, retrain, or reject under \emph{natural} concept drift, formulating
detection as a one-step Markov decision process. The control problem is
adjacent to ours and its policy space is genuinely learned rather than fixed,
but the pressure is distributional rather than adversarial.

\textbf{Benchmarks.} EMBER~\cite{anderson2018ember} remains the reference
static-PE feature set and the substrate for most of the above;
EMBER2024~\cite{joyce2025ember2024} extends it with a challenge set of files
that evaded commercial antivirus products, complementary to the adversarial
pressure we generate synthetically.

\textbf{Position.} We sit on top of this cluster rather than beside it. Our
attacker and defender are deliberately conventional; the contribution is that
every policy is measured under one harness, so a difference between two numbers
is attributable to the policy rather than to the evaluation setup.

\section{Threat Model and Formulation}

\textbf{Adversary.} A black-box evader with query access to the deployed
classifier's score, a bounded query budget per sample, and a repertoire of
functionality-preserving modifications. It observes neither the defender's
parameters, nor its training data, nor its retraining schedule.

\textbf{Defender.} A static-feature classifier that may retrain between rounds
on clean data plus any adversarial samples it has retained. It observes the
evasive samples produced against the \emph{previous} snapshot, not the
attacker's policy.

\textbf{The game.} Round $t$ proceeds: (i) the defender's parameters are frozen
as snapshot $D_t$; (ii) the attacker searches against $D_t$ over a held-out
malicious pool, producing evasive set $A_t$; (iii) the retention policy admits
some subset of $A_t$ into replay buffer $B_t$; (iv) a cadence rule decides
whether to retrain and a mode rule decides how, producing $D_{t+1}$. A
\emph{retraining policy} is the triple (cadence, retention, mode).

\textbf{Metrics.} Let $e_t$ be the fraction of the evaluation pool that $D_t$
scores as benign. We report \emph{settled evasion} $\evrate$, the mean of $e_t$
over the final $w=4$ rounds, and the \emph{oscillation index}
$\osc=\mathrm{std}(e_{T-w+1},\dots,e_T)$, which distinguishes a defender that
has converged from one whose evasion rate is still swinging. We separate
\emph{attack success}---the fraction of samples the defender initially caught
that the attacker flipped---from the defender's \emph{pre-existing false
negatives}. Conflating them credits the attacker with the classifier's own
misses, and Section~\ref{sec:mode} contains a case where that distinction is
the difference between ``the attack succeeded'' and ``the detector collapsed.''

\section{Benchmark Harness}
\label{sec:harness}

\textbf{Data.} EMBER-2018~\cite{anderson2018ember}, vectorised with the
official extractor to the canonical $2381$-dimensional representation. We draw
a balanced $8000$-sample training subsample and a held-out malicious evaluation
pool of $600$ from EMBER's own test split, enforced disjoint by SHA-256.
Features are standardised so a perturbation of a given magnitude is comparable
across dimensions of very different natural scale.

\textbf{Defender.} A histogram gradient-boosted tree ensemble, the algorithmic
counterpart of EMBER's LightGBM reference model, reaching $98.4\%$ clean
accuracy on held-out data, consistent with published EMBER
baselines~\cite{anderson2018ember}. Early stopping is pinned off; the reason is
a subtle confound given in Section~\ref{sec:calibration}.

\textbf{Attacker.} A \emph{mimicry} attacker in feature space. Each episode
draws a random benign exemplar as target and moves the malicious sample toward
it one feature block at a time, subject to the mutability constraints below.
This choice is empirical rather than aesthetic: our DQN and PPO agents plateau
well below it (Section~\ref{sec:calibration}).

\textbf{Attack surface.} The attacker may edit every feature block a
functionality-preserving modification demonstrably affects---byte and
byte-entropy histograms, strings, sections, imports, exports, general file
properties, and data directories---plus free-form header metadata such as
timestamps, version fields, and \texttt{sizeof} entries. Only the $40$
\emph{structural} header dimensions (target machine, COFF characteristics,
subsystem, PE magic) are frozen, leaving $2341$ of $2381$ dimensions editable.
Section~\ref{sec:calibration} shows why this is the single most consequential
choice in the design.

\textbf{Policies.} Cadence $\in$ \{every round, every third round,
threshold-triggered, never, minimax\}; retention $\in$ \{full replay, bounded
FIFO buffer, hardest-example mining\}; mode $\in$ \{refit from scratch,
warm-start\}.

\section{Calibration: What Had to Be Fixed First}
\label{sec:calibration}

Four results, each measured rather than assumed, materially constrain how such
an experiment must be built. We report them because two silently invalidate the
study if set wrongly, and neither is visible in low-dimensional synthetic data.
We regard this section as a contribution in its own right: these are failure
modes a co-evolution benchmark can exhibit while appearing to work.

\textbf{C1: The mutability assumption decides the outcome.} If the attacker is
barred from the \texttt{general}, \texttt{datadirectories} and \texttt{exports}
blocks---a restriction that looks conservative---then a classifier trained on
the frozen remainder \emph{alone} reaches $0.970$ accuracy. Adversarial
retraining then simply learns to lean on features the attacker can never touch:
evasion collapses to zero within two rounds and \emph{every} retraining policy
ties at zero. The reported outcome would be a property of the threat-model
encoding, not of the policy under study. Restricting the frozen set to the $40$
structural header dimensions lowers frozen-only accuracy to $0.769$ and keeps
the game contested. Because appending bytes provably changes file and virtual
size, and adding a section or import changes data-directory sizes and RVAs, the
permissive encoding is also the more faithful one.

\textbf{C2: Random perturbation is not a viable attack at this
dimensionality.} A set of random directions over ${\sim}10^3$ mutable features
yields ${\le}0.04$ attack success and, diagnostically, is \emph{insensitive to
step size}: a larger budget buys nothing, because a random vector in that many
dimensions is nearly orthogonal to any descent direction. Semantic mimicry
directions restore a monotone dependence on budget, the signature of an action
space that is doing work.

\textbf{C3: A fixed attack strategy yields a knockout, not a game.} With one
fixed mimicry direction set, evasion goes
$0.280\rightarrow0.003\rightarrow0.000$ and never recovers: the defender closes
a single narrow cone in one round. Redrawing the target exemplar per episode
restores gradual decay and leaves room for policies to differ. The lesson
generalises: a co-evolution benchmark measures the defence only if the
attacker's reachable set is not something the defender can memorise in one
round.

\textbf{C4: Reinforcement-learning attackers underperform stochastic mimicry.}
DQN reaches $0.104$ attack success at $1000$ cumulative episodes against
$0.194$ for mimicry, and only $0.018$ in a full co-evolution round; PPO is
weaker and non-monotone in its training budget. The mechanism is structural
rather than a tuning failure: a greedy policy repeatedly applies one argmax
action and therefore edits a single feature block, whereas a stochastic policy
accumulates movement across all of them. We therefore use the stronger attacker
for the main study. It also means we do not run the attacker as a factorial
axis: an agent pinned near the floor cannot discriminate between defensive
policies, so every retention strategy would post a near-zero evasion rate
whether or not the conclusion generalises, and the resulting null would be
uninformative by construction.

Two further confounds are worth recording because both are silent. First,
scikit-learn enables early stopping above $10{,}000$ training samples by
default; here the training set is clean data plus retained adversarial samples,
so that threshold is \emph{policy-dependent}. A policy that retains more, or
one that fails and therefore generates more evasions, crosses it while a capped
or successful policy never does, and past it the model fits far fewer trees.
Second, wall-clock retraining time is not a usable cost unit across runs
sharing a machine: we measured a $3.8\times$ spread in seconds-per-retrain
between studies performing identical work. All cost claims here are therefore
stated in retrains and base learners fitted, both exact, with wall-clock
reported only from a controlled sequential measurement.

\section{Experimental Design}

Independent variables: cadence $\times$ retention $\times$ mode, fully crossed
($3\times3\times2$), each replicated over five seeds, at a fixed horizon of
eight rounds. Early stopping on convergence is disabled so every policy is
evaluated over an identical horizon and costs remain comparable. Replay
capacity is set to $200$, chosen to \emph{bind}: with an oversized cap all
three retention strategies collect identical data and the factor cannot
differentiate at all.

Baselines: a \textbf{frozen classifier} that never retrains, the lower bound
implicit in single-round evasion work; and a \textbf{minimax alternation}
baseline in the style of Ebrahimi \emph{et al.}~\cite{ebrahimi2022arl}, in
which the defender retrains on alternate rounds while the attacker strengthens
on the rounds in between. For a non-learning attacker we model
attacker-strengthening as an escalating query budget, and describe this as a
minimal stand-in rather than a reimplementation.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{The game is contested}

Fig.~\ref{fig:dynamics} shows a representative run. The attacker opens by
flipping $78.3\%$ of the samples the defender caught; adversarial retraining
suppresses this to $0.037$ by round eight without eroding clean accuracy, which
stays within $[0.980,0.984]$ throughout. Mean queries per sample rise from
$31.4$ to $60.2$: evasion becomes measurably \emph{harder}, not merely rarer.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_dynamics}
\caption{Co-evolution dynamics for every-round retraining with full replay.
Top: evasion, attack success, and clean accuracy per round. Bottom: attacker
query cost, plotted on its own axis rather than as a second $y$-scale.}
\label{fig:dynamics}
\end{figure}

\subsection{The frozen lower bound}

Against a classifier that never retrains, the attacker settles at
$\evrate=0.829\pm0.019$. The best policy reduces this by $94.9\%$ to
$0.042\pm0.003$. The frozen baseline also exhibits \emph{low} oscillation
($0.011$), which is why $\osc$ must be read jointly with $\evrate$: a
statically bad detector is stable precisely because it is not responding.

\subsection{Retention dominates cadence; cadence is undetectable}

Table~\ref{tab:policies} and Fig.~\ref{fig:policies} give all nine
cadence--retention cells at fixed mode. The three retention levels separate
cleanly; the three cadences do not.

egin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig3_marginals}
\caption{Marginal effect of each factor, averaging over the other. Averaging
isolates one variable at a time, which is the point of a factorial design
rather than a series of pairwise comparisons: retention spans a sixfold range
with tight seed variance, while the three cadences differ by less than their
own standard deviations.}
\label{fig:marginals}
\end{figure}

Averaging over one factor isolates the other (Fig.~\ref{fig:marginals}). A
two-way ANOVA on this balanced design attributes $\omega^2=0.947$ to
retention ($F(2,36)=375.5$, $p<10^{-24}$) and essentially nothing to cadence
($F(2,36)=0.77$, $p=0.472$, $\omega^2=-0.001$), with no significant interaction
($p=0.810$). Tukey HSD separates all three retention levels ($p<10^{-5}$) and
no cadence pair ($p>0.95$).

\textbf{Robustness.} Levene's test does not reject equal variances
($p=0.259$), but Shapiro--Wilk rejects normality of residuals ($p=0.0023$).
Welch's ANOVA relaxes the assumption that \emph{held} rather than the one that
failed, so we use a rank-based check instead: Kruskal--Wallis gives $H=35.15$,
$p=2.3\times10^{-8}$ for retention and $H=0.47$, $p=0.79$ for cadence, and
Dunn's test with Holm correction separates all three retention levels
($p\le0.016$) and no cadence pair ($p=1.00$). Both factors reach the same
verdict as the parametric analysis.

\subsection{The retention effect is a capacity threshold}
\label{sec:capacity}

Retention as configured varies two things at once: how many adversarial samples
are kept, and which are discarded when the cap binds. Full replay is unbounded
while the others are capped, so the headline gap conflates the two. Sweeping
the cap separates them (Table~\ref{tab:capacity}, Fig.~\ref{fig:capacity}).

\begin{table}[t]
\caption{Capacity gradient, mean $\pm$ std over five seeds, every-round
cadence, refit from scratch.}
\label{tab:capacity}
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Replay capacity & FIFO buffer & Hardest-example mining \\
\midrule
$200$     & $0.3110\pm0.0242$ & $0.3761\pm0.0577$ \\
$800$     & $0.0425\pm0.0021$ & $0.0428\pm0.0034$ \\
unbounded & \multicolumn{2}{c}{$0.0421\pm0.0027$ (full replay)} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig4_capacity}
\caption{Capacity gradient. Raising the cap from $200$ to $800$ closes the
entire gap to unbounded replay (dashed line, shaded $\pm1$\,std) and
simultaneously erases the difference between eviction rules.}
\label{fig:capacity}
\end{figure}

Raising the cap from $200$ to $800$ moves FIFO from $0.311$ to $0.0425$ and
mining from $0.376$ to $0.0428$---both statistically indistinguishable from
unbounded replay ($0.0421\pm0.0027$) and from each other. Full replay's
apparent superiority is therefore \emph{capacity}: it is the only configuration
whose cap never binds. Above the threshold, which adversarial samples are
discarded stops mattering entirely.

Below the threshold the eviction rule does matter, in the direction opposite to
intuition: plain FIFO ($0.311$) outperforms hardest-example mining ($0.376$),
and mining is also the most oscillatory policy in the study ($\osc=0.056$).
Selecting for the deepest evasions concentrates the buffer on a narrow region
of input space and discards the diversity the defender needs to generalise.

\subsection{Retraining mode dominates when added as a third factor}
\label{sec:mode}

Extending the design with mode gives a balanced $3\times3\times2$ factorial
over $90$ runs, and reorders the conclusion (Table~\ref{tab:anova3},
Fig.~\ref{fig:mode}). Warm-starting settles at $\evrate=0.694$ against $0.245$
for refitting and oscillates twice as much. Even its best cell ($0.503$) is
closer to never retraining ($0.829$) than to the best refit policy ($0.042$).
Kruskal--Wallis agrees ($H=45.25$, $p=1.7\times10^{-11}$).

Source & SS & df & $F$ & $p$ & $\omega^2$ \\

Retention & $0.6671$ & $2$ & $11.25$ & $5.6\times10^{-5}$ & $0.076$ \\
Cadence & $0.0261$ & $2$ & $0.44$ & $0.645$ & $-0.004$ \\
Residual & $2.1355$ & $72$ & & & \\
\bottomrule

\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig6_mode}
\caption{Refitting from scratch (solid) versus warm-starting (hatched) at each
retention level. Warm-starting is worse everywhere, and its spread across seeds
is far larger.}
\label{fig:mode}
\end{figure}

\textbf{The failure is collapse, not slow learning.} Instrumenting the worst
seed reveals what the aggregate hides. Clean accuracy falls monotonically
$0.979\rightarrow0.954\rightarrow0.844\rightarrow0.659$, and by round four the
pre-existing false-negative rate reaches $0.870$: the detector classifies
$87\%$ of \emph{unmodified} malware as benign before the attack begins, and
attacker queries fall to $2.5$ per sample because there is nothing left to
evade. The apparent $\evrate\approx1.0$ is therefore not attacker skill but
detector destruction---a distinction visible only because attack success is
reported separately from pre-existing false negatives. The mechanism is that
mimicry endpoints lie \emph{inside} the benign region, so the buffer teaches
that points indistinguishable from benign files are malicious. A refit
rebalances against that contradiction each round; a warm start accumulates it
across $3902$ such samples until the boundary degenerates.

\textbf{Instability is a finding, not a caveat.} Testing dispersion on
cell-centred residuals---so the arms' very different means cannot leak into the
estimate---warm-starting's run-to-run variance is $61\times$ that of refitting
($95\%$ CI $23$--$157\times$; Levene $W=20.47$, $p=3.5\times10^{-5}$;
Brown--Forsythe is quoted because the residuals are not normal). Refitting
lands in $0.038$--$0.043$ across seeds for the winning policy; warm-starting
ranges $0.252$--$0.999$. A policy whose outcome depends that strongly on a seed
is not merely worse, it is unbudgetable.

\textbf{Capacity does not rescue it.} Granting the warm-started model five
times the incremental trees per round moves settled evasion from $0.724$ to
$0.711$: no recovery, at roughly five times the fitting cost and five times the
prediction cost the attacker pays on every query. A single-round diagnostic had
suggested capacity would suffice---refitting catches $100\%$ of $481$ evasive
samples where warm-starting at equal incremental budget catches $84.4\%$---but
the deficit compounds across rounds faster than added capacity corrects it.

\textbf{Clean accuracy of the winning policy.} For contrast, the winning policy
holds clean accuracy flat across the entire run. Over all $40$ (seed, round)
observations it stays within $0.9756$--$0.9862$, with a net drift of $-0.0012$
and a mean slope of $-7.9\times10^{-5}$ per round, while the replay buffer
nearly doubles from $494$ to $873$ samples. Robustness is not being bought with
false positives.

\subsection{Cost, and the minimax baseline}

In exact units, retraining every third round performs $3$ refits against
$8$---a $2.67\times$ reduction in retraining work that holds on any
machine---for a settled-evasion penalty of $0.007$. Since cadence has no
detectable main effect, this is the operating point we recommend. Under
controlled sequential measurement, refits of this size cost $14.6$--$16.5$\,s
each.

Minimax alternation settles at $0.088\pm0.005$ with $\osc=0.043\pm0.009$,
performing $4$ refits. It is thus \emph{cheaper} than retraining every round
while accepting roughly twice the evasion and four times the oscillation: a
genuine trade rather than a dominated policy. The elevated oscillation is the
alternation itself---the attacker escalating on rounds the defender sits
out---and is exactly what $\osc$ is designed to expose.
Fig.~\ref{fig:frontier} places every policy and both baselines on the
robustness--cost plane.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig5_frontier}
\caption{Robustness versus retraining cost. Lower is more robust, left is
cheaper. Hollow markers are the frozen and minimax baselines.}
\label{fig:frontier}
\end{figure}

\section{Discussion}

The practical reading is blunt. A vendor spending an adversarial retraining
budget should spend it on \emph{how} the model is refit and on \emph{retaining
enough} adversarial data---not on retraining more often. Within this design,
tripling the retraining frequency is statistically indistinguishable from not
doing so, while warm-starting instead of refitting moves settled evasion by a
factor of nearly three and risks destroying the detector outright.

The capacity result simplifies the design problem rather than complicating it.
Because performance saturates---$800$ retained samples already match unbounded
replay---the operative question is not \emph{which} adversarial samples to keep
but whether the buffer is above threshold. Above it, eviction policy is a free
choice; below it, the intuitively appealing heuristic is the worst one. We
expect the threshold to scale with the diversity of the attack rather than
being universal, and locating it for a deployment is a cheap one-dimensional
sweep.

Two methodological points generalise beyond this dataset. First, a co-evolution
benchmark measures the defence only if the attacker's reachable set cannot be
memorised in a single round; a fixed attack strategy produces a knockout that
reads as a defensive success (C3). Second, the encoding of which features the
adversary may modify is not a detail of the threat model but the dominant
determinant of the result (C1), and deserves to be reported and justified as
prominently as the model architecture. We encourage future work in this area to
report frozen-feature-only accuracy as a standard diagnostic: if a classifier
restricted to immutable features already performs near the full model, the
experiment cannot measure what it claims to.

\section{Limitations}

The attack is \emph{feature-space}: the adversary perturbs EMBER vectors rather
than PE files, so the reported rates are not measured against binaries verified
to still execute. Bridging to the problem
space~\cite{pierazzi2020problemspace,tsingenopoulos2024raid} requires a malware
corpus under institutional and legal control and is future work. We expect the
policy \emph{ordering} to survive that transition, since none of the three
factors is specific to how perturbations are realised, but absolute rates would
change.

The main study uses a stochastic mimicry attacker because our RL agents apply
substantially weaker pressure (C4). We therefore claim the ordering holds
\emph{for an attacker strong enough to create meaningful pressure};
establishing that it also holds under a strong \emph{learned} attacker requires
an agent competitive with mimicry, which our calibration suggests is an open
problem rather than a matter of tuning.

Results are on one corpus, one defender family, an eight-round horizon, and an
$8000$-sample subsample. The cadence null is best read as ``no detectable
effect at this power'' rather than a demonstrated equivalence; a longer horizon
might expose differences eight rounds cannot.

\section{Conclusion}

We ran the controlled comparison the iterated-malware-detection literature has
been missing: one harness, one attacker, one metric set, and the retraining
policy as the independent variable. How the detector is refit dominates what it
is refit on, which in turn dominates how often it is refit---and cadence, the
knob most naturally exposed to operators, is not statistically detectable at
all. The retention effect is a capacity threshold rather than a selection
heuristic, and the most intuitive heuristic is the worst performer below that
threshold. Warm-started retraining is not merely inferior but unstable, and can
collapse the detector to the point where it misclassifies most unmodified
malware. A minimax-alternation baseline is a genuine cost--robustness trade
rather than a dominated policy. We release the harness, the calibration
constraints, and all run artifacts so the comparison can be extended to new
policies, attackers, and corpora.

\section*{Reproducibility}

Harness, configurations, analysis scripts, and every result file are released.
All figures are regenerated from the committed artifacts by a single script and
no reported number is hand-entered; a figure whose source study is incomplete
is skipped rather than drawn from partial data. The calibration results of
Section~\ref{sec:calibration} are documented separately so the constraints they
impose are reusable.
